claim:
Let \(X=(\mathbb R^2,N)\) be the real Banach plane
\[
N(s,t)=
\begin{cases}
\max\{|s|,|t|\},&st\ge0,\\
\sqrt{s^2+t^2},&st\le0.
\end{cases}
\]
For \(\varepsilon\in[0,1)\), write \(u\perp_D^\varepsilon v\) when
\[
N(u+\lambda v)\ge\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2}\,N(u)
\qquad(\lambda\in\mathbb R).
\]
Then the least \(\varepsilon\) such that
\[
x\perp_B y\Longrightarrow y\perp_D^\varepsilon x
\qquad(x,y\in X)
\]
is
\[
\varepsilon_D(X)=\frac1{\sqrt2}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\inf_{\substack{x,y\in S_X\\x\perp_B y}}
\inf_{\lambda\in\mathbb R}N(y+\lambda x)
=
\frac1{\sqrt2}.
\]
Equality is attained by
\[
x=(1,1),\qquad y=(1,0),
\]
and by the norm symmetries. Thus this canonical mixed square--circle example has a sharp global modified-Dragomir symmetry constant even though the same example is used in the literature to show complete failure of global Chmieliński approximate symmetry.

correctness.rationale: The unit sphere is exhaustively split into smooth square edges, smooth circular arcs, and square corners. Square edges give \(d=1/\sqrt{1+t^2}\ge1/\sqrt2\). Circular arcs give \(d=(1+r^2)/(1+r)\ge2(\sqrt2-1)>1/\sqrt2\). Square corners give \(d=(c+s)/\sqrt2\ge1/\sqrt2\), with equality at coordinate-axis companions. The dual norm and quotient-distance formula are explicit, and \(x=(1,1)\), \(y=(1,0)\) realizes equality.
risks: The theorem is specific to real scalars and dimension two.
The modified Dragomir normalization \(\sqrt{1-\varepsilon^2}\) is essential.

value.rationale: The source paper itself uses this mixed square--circle plane to separate two notions of approximate symmetry: the C-version fails globally. Computing the sharp D-parameter on the same canonical example therefore quantifies the contrast between the two approximation theories rather than merely adding another table entry. The extremizer is structurally informative: the worst reverse asymmetry occurs at a square corner against a coordinate axis, while every circular-arc Birkhoff pair is uniformly better.
risks: The result is one exact benchmark rather than a family-wide formula.
